subject: desertOasisDiorama
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: desert oasis with palms, tents and camels.
Style: low-poly whimsical mix.
reasoning:
I'm planning a desert oasis diorama scene with palms, tents, and camels, aiming for a long but correct low-poly TypeScript module. Since it's a diorama category, I'm treating scenery as plain objects while giving the camels proper skeletal structure since they're creatures.

I'm working out real-world scale — camels around 2m tall, palms around 4.5m, with a sand-dune plinth roughly 3.2 × 2.4m centered on the origin — and reviewing the SDK's builder, joint, and chain functions I'll need to construct it.

Reviewing the rest of the available build functions — sweep, loft, part, surface sampling, along/ring iterators, cards, decals, extrude, lathe, membrane, spike, and pose — along with the IK limb helper I'll use for the camels' legs and jaw articulation.

Everything imports from a single "agentic-3js-builder" package, with optional kits like toon available separately. I'm weighing whether a cel-shading toon kit fits the whimsical low-poly aesthetic for the camels and sand, but leaning toward keeping dependencies minimal to limit risk, so I may skip the toon kit entirely and stick with the core builder primitives.

For the ground, I'm thinking a rounded sand-topped plinth slab works best since the oasis setting calls for visible sand, keeping the base footprint within the diorama bounds.

On top I'll add a thin sand-colored cylinder layer painted with mottled texture and ripples, then shape dunes at the edges using scaled sphere meshes or lathed blobs to give the mounds some whimsical variation.

For the oasis, I'm planning a flat cylinder disc as a water pool sitting at sand level, colored blue with a simple paint, possibly adding a subtle glow for shimmer while keeping the overall look clean and understated.

For palms, I'm thinking of building trunks as chained catmull curves with swept bark-banded geometry, and fronds as extruded leaflet shapes attached at the crown joint, drooping outward from branching stalks.

I'm thinking simpler now: a frond is just a curved chain of a few joints forming an arc-and-droop shape, with the blade built as a thickened extrusion placed along that chain's direction, keeping thickness minimal for a stylized blocky look.

That membrane approach works nicely as a palm leaf: two catmull-path edges forming the blade silhouette, with a midrib sweep and scallop taper for the leaflets. Even better, I could make one edge zigzag outward and inward against a straight midrib edge, creating a comb-like, leaflet-toothed frond shape that reads as much more palm-like.

For the zigzag, I realize a smooth catmull curve risks looping at sharp teeth, so a polyline is safer for the jagged edge while still working fine as a membrane path. I'll keep it manageable with a single membrane between a left zigzag edge and a right zigzag edge (both offset from a central frond curve), generating the point samples programmatically rather than hand-placing them.

Each sample point alternates a "tooth" scale factor to create the serrated leaflet look, with width tapering along the frond length, and both edges running base-to-tip so the membrane works correctly. For bones, I'll pass the frond chain itself so the path follows it naturally rather than defaulting to nearest-joint behavior.

For the crown-to-trunk connection, I'm defining the trunk as a chain with enough point names to give it a tip joint at the very top, then attaching the crown joint there so the fronds parent correctly off the trunk's apex.

Now I'm figuring out the bark texture for the trunk — using a paint function that generates ring-like bands along the trunk's height to mimic bark segments.

Then I'm shifting focus to the camel skeleton: hips, a spine/chest chain, neck and head with jaw, four legs with knee/hock joints, tail, and humps modeled as spheres or sweeps.

Now I'm figuring out which bones should drive the body loft — probably the spine and hips chain — before sketching out the full camel rig layout with the length running along the z-axis.

I'm estimating the proportions of a dromedary camel: shoulder height around 1.9m, body length around 2.2m, and working out approximate joint heights for the legs (hip, knee, hock). I'm planning a helper function to compute joint positions offset by the camel's overall position and yaw rotation, so I can mirror leg pieces consistently.

I'm deriving the rotation math so a camel's local forward direction correctly maps to world coordinates based on its yaw angle, verifying with local z and x axis test cases to confirm the rotation formula is consistent before applying it to all body points.

Now I'm planning the rig structure for the camel: defining limbs and joints using `at`/`aim` points, then realizing the scene constraint that only one root joint is allowed across the whole scene—so each camel's hips joint must be parented under a shared scene root rather than existing as independent roots.

Since names must stay unique across camels, I'll prefix each camel's joints (like "c1") and start sketching the per-camel skeleton — hips positioned at a local offset from the base, parented to it, with forward aim to build out the rest of the chain.

Working out the spine curve from hips to chest, then a separate neck chain rising up to the head, and a muzzle point extending forward from the head joint. I'm laying out the actual coordinate arrays now for the catmull-rom spine path...

Jaw joint placement near head, with skull and muzzle as separate parts attached to the head bone. I'm reconsidering the approach: rather than sweeping the neck and head, maybe loft the body along the spine, sweep only the neck chain, and represent the head as a simpler scaled sphere or extruded shape instead.

I'm working out the head loft with 3-4 stations along the head joint axis from skull to muzzle, then simplifying by defining all key points explicitly and building the body loft along the spine centerline from hips to chest with varying widths and heights at each station, skinning it to the spine chain via the bone option.

For the hump, I'm considering a sphere scaled to shape it, positioned on the back joint of the spine near the body surface, checking whether the scaled radius would properly overlap the body loft's top height given the width/height parameters used for stations.

Now I'm thinking through the legs—placing hip and shoulder joints at estimated local offsets, then using limb geometry from hip to foot target on the ground, with segment lengths sketched out roughly like a camel's thigh and shin proportions.

For bending direction, front legs knee forward and hind legs bend back, and each limb's resulting points get chained into named joints (hip, knee, foot) to build the skeletal path for the leg.

Now I'm working out parent attachment: hind legs should parent to the hips joint, front legs to somewhere along the spine or chest, since the spine chain exposes its own joints array to attach limbs to.

Actually, simpler to just have a single root joint per camel at the origin, with the spine chain parented directly to that base joint.

For legs, I'm figuring out foot placement: the pad should sit just above ground with the hoof as a small piece at the tip, so target y lands around 0.06. The hip roots for the legs need to sit inside the body volume—hind legs around (±0.3, 1.2, -0.5) and front legs around (±0.3, 1.25, 0.35)—then I need to work out matching foot targets below.

Checking reach distances, I'm picking bone lengths around 0.6-0.64 per segment so hind and front legs both comfortably reach their ground targets with a slight knee bend rather than overextending or falling short—adjusting root heights slightly (hind hip ~1.2, front chest ~1.28) to keep both legs within range of a two-bone IK chain that bends naturally at the knee.

Now I'm setting up bend directions for each leg's IK chain, with front legs bending forward and hind legs (camel hocks) bending backward, then placing small pad/hoof geometry at each foot tip. I'm also sketching out a tail chain extending back and down from the rump, parented to the spine, with a tapering radius along its length.

Next I'm defining the neck chain as a three-point path from chest to head, parented to the spine's tip joint since they share that connection point, and setting up the sweep geometry along this chain to give the neck its shape.

For the head, I'm planning a lofted shape with several stations moving from the back of the skull through the skull itself down to the muzzle front and tip, each with its own width and height to carve out the skull-to-muzzle profile.

I'll rig the loft to the head joint at the tip of the neck chain so it stays rigid with that single joint, which should be valid since sweep/loft accepts a joint as the bone parameter. For character, I want bigger expressive ears as extruded leaf shapes with tufts, plus eye decals applied to the head's surface using a surface helper on the head mesh.

Working out the eye placement, I'm positioning them symmetrically around a head center point using azimuth/elevation angles matching the toon example convention, where azimuth 90 corresponds to +X. Since my sign convention puts the left eye at +X, I'll mirror that decal to match the model's right-eye artwork, then apply both eye decals using the hit's surface normal for orientation and matching size parameters.

Now I'm turning to the ears, which need to be extruded leaf-shaped outlines positioned relative to the head bone using local offsets for left/up/back placement, oriented in a vertical plane so the thickness axis runs sideways along the head.

Positioning ears using local offsets, with s=1 placing it left and s=-1 for the mirrored right side, matching the convention used in the toon example — same x direction reused for both ears since the mirroring happens via the sign flip.

For the nose, I'll keep it simple: a small sphere attached to the head bone, positioned forward and slightly down from the head's local origin to sit at the muzzle front, though I still need to pin down exact head loft coordinates.

Laying out head station points for skull, muzzle, and tip with approximate widths and heights, all lofted rigidly on the head bone so positioning stays fixed. Now I'm placing the eyes relative to the skull center.

For the jaw, I'm setting up a separate joint so the mouth can open, placing it below the head joint and aiming it toward the muzzle, then building the lower jaw as a capsule shape attached to that bone.

Joint names need to follow a strict alphanumeric pattern, so I'll prefix each camel's joints like "c1" to keep them unique. For the scene, I'm thinking three camels: two kneeling near the oasis and one standing to drink, which means working out folded leg poses where the front legs tuck under the chest with feet targeting near the ground but forward of the knees.

Instead of risking awkward kneeling poses, I'm leaning toward having all three camels standing but varying their head positions — one dipping its head down toward the pool as if drinking. I'm figuring out how to tilt the head/neck joint using a pose rotation around an axis so the head angles downward realistically, testing which direction counts as positive rotation for that bone.

I'll simplify the poses: drinking camel gets head angled down, grazing camel gets head raised, and the other two stand neutral. I'm placing the pool at the diorama's center-back with palms and tents nearby, camels clustered near the water. Now I'm thinking through the Bedouin tent shapes — rectangular or cone-like structures.

Prototyping tent geometry...

I'm thinking the flat-faced lathe gives the tent a clean pyramid shape sitting on sand, but maybe it needs a tall tip pole and a door flap extruded as a triangle in front for whimsy -- perhaps leaning toward a long, low Bedouin-style tent instead of a strict pyramid.

I'll throw in colorful cushion boxes for whimsy, then figure out tent stripes using a custom paint function based on angle position for a striped canvas look.

For the oasis scene, I'm planning 3-4 palm trees with leaning trunks and 7 fronds each, roughly 36 parts total, plus around 75 parts for the camels to keep the overall budget reasonable.

Now I'm thinking through texture choices — around 5-12 textures total, including a patterned cloth texture for tent flaps applied as a decal, figuring out how to position it on the tent's flat face using the right surface normal and anchor point.

I'm working out the lathe geometry's spin parameter to orient a face of the pyramid tent toward +Z, so the decal lands flush on a front-facing surface rather than straddling an edge.

Instead of texturing the lathe directly, I'm considering a simpler approach: adding a draped triangular flap as the tent door, then applying a patterned texture using a plane decal projected onto the sloped front face so it conforms to the surface properly.

I'm now planning out the texture set: a zigzag tent band pattern for decaling tents, a toon-style anime eye texture for camels, and a geometric blanket pattern for camel saddles.

For the blanket I'm weighing whether to apply it as a flat box part or decal directly onto the camel body loft near the hump base — the decal approach seems more whimsical and should work fine on a loft surface. Then I'm adding a pennant flag texture for tent poles using a simple plane, and a wooden oasis sign with painted "OASIS" text rendered via SVG.

Next I'm thinking through a rug — a textured plane laid flat on the sand inside the tent, oriented facing upward so it reads correctly from a top-down view, placed slightly above ground level to avoid z-fighting. I'm also considering adding grass-tuft cards with SVG textures near the oasis edge for extra whimsy.

Then I'm settling the palette: warm peach and ochre tones for sand with a cool lilac shade for cel-style shadows, plus greens for palms, brown for trunks, aqua for water, and a canvas tone for the tent, while planning a mottled sand paint with subtle ripple lines using sine waves to suggest dunes.

I'm thinking about using the toon kit's cel shading helper broadly across camels, palms, and tents so everything shares the same whimsical cartoon look, including wrapping nested paints like stripes inside cel so shadows derive automatically from the underlying pattern.

For lanterns and water, I'm planning to add glow effects on flat-colored parts for a gentle shimmer, then sketch out the module's export structure with a default build function and meta object, plus the necessary imports from three and the builder kit.

The glow kit's emissive map assignment should work fine internally. For createBuilder, I'll set options with name "oasis" and a paintSize of 2048 for finer detail, keeping within the 4096 atlas max.

With roughly seven textures at 256-512px plus the paint sheet, I'm checking texel density across the painted diorama area (~15 m²) and confirming 1024 resolution gives about 4.6mm per texel, which is sufficient — I'll stick with 1024. Now I'm starting to design the sand base, beginning with a cylindrical plinth geometry for the diorama.

I'm deciding parts need explicit bone assignment, defaulting scenery pieces to the root joint since there's no nearby joint otherwise. I'm also considering adding a brass plaque reading "OASIS" on the plinth's front face, positioning a flat plane textured with text at the cylinder's radius so it sits flush against the front, accounting for the fact that a 12-sided cylinder has flat facets to align the plaque against.

Still figuring out plinth geometry...

Actually, decal seems like the better approach here—it projects directly onto the curved surface rather than requiring manual geometry alignment, so I should use that for the plaque instead.

For the ground, I'm layering a wooden plinth base, then a sand disc on top, with several scaled spheres sitting on the sand to form dunes, keeping them sized so they don't overhang the diorama's edge.

Now I'm setting up a recessed pool: a thin water disc positioned at an adjusted height, carefully offsetting the sand layer's y-coordinates so the pool sits believably within the sand surface.

Adding scenery details...

Adjusting card sizing and color...

I'll default to the root bone for safety, then plan four palm trees positioned around the pool and along the back of the diorama, designing a palm-building function that takes base position, height, lean, and seed parameters.

For the trunk, I'm sketching a curved path through control points using a Catmull-Rom spline from base to top, naming the segments trunkA through crown, and tapering the sweep radius so it's wider at the flared base and narrower near the top.

For sides I'll keep the default polygon count for a low-poly look. I'm painting the trunk with alternating light and dark rings based on position along the sweep, giving it a whimsical striped texture, and then adding small coconut-colored sphere clusters near the crown joint for frond stubs.

Now I'm figuring out the fronds themselves: eight radiating around the top at even angles with some jitter, each built as a curved path from the crown outward and drooping downward using a catmull-rom spline through control points, then widening into a blade shape by offsetting left and right edges along a perpendicular side vector.

That horizontal perpendicular offset gives a flat blade in plan view, like a V-shaped spread typical of palm fronds. I'll let the two side widths differ for asymmetry.

Defining the arch profile...

Refining the width formula...

For the leaflet teeth I'm alternating sample heights between full and 0.55 along both edges to create a jagged silhouette, resampled by arc length into membrane rows. The frond chain uses a bone chain parented to the crown with a resample count, so the named spans get distributed along the curve's points.

Naming the chains and joints needs care to avoid collisions — I'm worried the default auto-suffix pattern could produce ugly or ambiguous names, so it's better to pass explicit name arrays for each joint instead of relying on generated suffixes.

Thinking through the points count for the frond path: with a 5-point path (4 spans), using 3 explicit names means the count won't line up with spans or spans+tip, so names get spread by arc length instead — that works fine. For the midrib, I'll sweep along the frond chain with a taper so the radius shrinks from base to tip, colored as the stem. For the leaf membrane, I'll pass arrays of point coordinates tied to the frond chain, paint it in the leaf color with cel shading, and let thickness default to roughly 2% of the leaf width.

For the leaflet shading, I want alternating light/dark bands running along the frond's length to suggest a V-shaped vein pattern, using the membrane's local along/across coordinates to decide which band each point falls in. I'm wrapping that banded paint inside the cel shader so it still picks up directional shading, and I need to make sure the across/along parameter gets threaded through correctly when the cel paint calls into the nested banding paint.

Now I'm shifting to designing the tents using a lathe shape — a low pyramidal outline (square cross-section via 4 segments spun 45°) with a base width around 2.4m and height near 1.5m to match a low, wide Bedouin-tent silhouette, setting it at a tent center position and binding it to the root bone with a tent-specific paint.

I also need a front door decal — considering using a dark arch-shaped texture decal projected onto the pyramid's front face, which requires computing that face's normal (roughly pointing up and outward at about 0.78y/0.62z based on the base apothem and height geometry) so the decal projects correctly onto the sloped tent wall.

There's some risk if the tent's spin orientation doesn't match the expected front-facing alignment, since the decal projects along its direction and could miss the intended face entirely. I'll accept that risk and proceed with the decal approach for a door, plus add a tent pole with a brass tip and a small pennant flag card mounted at the top using a plane with a flag texture.

For the flag itself, I'm weighing options since textured planes only render front-facing — double-sided cards could work better, but the orientation logic around facing axis versus card growth direction is getting tangled, so I'll simplify by making the pennant an extruded shape with painted stripes instead of a texture, avoiding the card complexity entirely. Now I'm cataloging the full texture set I'll need: an eye texture, a tent trim band, a camel blanket pattern, grass cards, a plaque sign reading "OASIS," and a rug texture.

For the rug I'm placing a plane geometry just above the sand so it reads as a carpet seen from above, nudging its height slightly to avoid z-fighting with the sand surface, and noting that since the pattern is symmetric the exact rotation doesn't matter. I'm also starting to lay out camel positions relative to a central pool, figuring out radius and placement so the first camel appears to be drinking at the water's edge.

I'm reconsidering the overall footprint — three palms, two tents, three camels feels cramped on a 4.2m plinth, so I'm thinking about enlarging the base to roughly 2.6m radius (about 5.2m across) to give everything breathing room while keeping camels around 2.1m tall and palms around 4.5m tall, since the brief calls for real-world scale on the diorama's subject rather than a toy-sized miniature.

Now I'm sketching out the actual layout: a pool centered slightly off-axis with a rocky ring, four palm trees of varying heights (2.8 to 4.4m) placed around and behind the pool, two tents positioned to the sides facing the same direction since the lathe geometry keeps them axis-aligned, and camels positioned near the pool edge and tents with specific facing angles — one drinking at the water's edge turned toward the pool, another standing near a tent at a different yaw angle.

I'm working out the camel body proportions and pivot points, checking that the drinking camel's head position lands correctly over the pool water when I account for its forward-facing orientation, and now I'm figuring out how to pose the neck and head joints so the drinking camel's muzzle dips down toward the water realistically.

Since bending the neck accurately is getting too complicated to guarantee, I'm deciding to simplify: skip the drinking pose entirely and just have camel 1 stand with its head raised instead.

I realize neck1, neck2, and head form a chain, so posing neck1 rotates everything below it around the chest joint, swinging head and neck2 together—meaning the head drops down since it's roughly 0.7 units out from that pivot point.

I'm estimating final head height isn't critical to nail exactly, so I'll just go with a simple downward-forward direction vector for a drinking/grazing pose, accepting some imprecision since the neck might slightly intersect the body but should look fine visually.

Now I'm thinking through how the neck skinning actually works — the sweep vertices near the neck1 joint likely blend with the parent chest joint, so posing neck1 should bend the neck smoothly without breaking the mesh. I want to avoid worrying too much about exact geometry and focus instead on making sure the API calls themselves are valid, since errors are more likely to come from misusing the joint/chain signatures than from the pose math.

I'm going through the remaining API signatures to confirm argument shapes: chains accept a path and options like up, twist, group, and naming; sweep takes a radius (number, pair, or function) plus styling options; loft takes station definitions with width/height; part takes geometry, color, and placement options including scale as an array; stick attaches geometry onto a target; and surface provides an `.around().at()` query that returns a hit or possibly null, which I'll need to handle carefully.

I'm also noting decal, extrude, lathe, membrane, rod, capsule, spike, and cards signatures, confirming that rod-like functions take radius before color and options, plus a `frame(at, dir, up?)` helper for orienting placements. Now I'm thinking through how to position extra eyes on the surface.

For surface queries, I should create `b.surface(headLoft)` right after building the head loft mesh, before adding ears or other children, so I avoid ambiguity about which meshes get captured — the loft call returns a Sweep-like object that surface can accept directly.

Now I'm working out eye placement: using a decal positioned near the head's side station (around w .36, so roughly .18 radius), with mirroring for symmetry and a small lift so the eyes read as big and whimsical rather than flat. I'm also thinking about glow for the lanterns and considering a countershaded coat color for the camel body — tan on top fading to cream on the belly — to give it some visual depth.

For the saddle blanket, I'm figuring out how to decal it onto the hump's back using a downward ray hit to find the top surface point, then orienting the decal's up vector along world Z since the dir vector points straight up, which otherwise would be degenerate — hoping the system orthogonalizes it correctly. I'm also checking where the hump sits relative to the body loft's top height to make sure the blanket sits naturally across the back.

Actually a thin box works better as a saddle blanket since all six faces can show the texture, so I'll place it as a flat box around (0, 1.82) on the back.

Checking the geometry though: at spine z=-0.45 the body top sits around y=1.65, but the hump sphere there extends down to about z=-0.46, meaning the blanket box might clip through the hump surface. I need to adjust the blanket's position or the hump's radius so they don't overlap awkwardly.

Good enough for now -- I'll place a small colored box as a draped blanket beneath the hump, using a texture so it reads as a patterned fabric rather than solid color.

Next I'm thinking through the camel's head attachment via the loft/bone system, then adding palm trees, coconuts, a crown sphere, and small foot pads as spheres scaled to look like hoof pads, each attached to the foot joint bones.

For the tail, I'm adding a small brown tuft sphere at the tip. For the legs, I'm sweeping a tapered profile along each limb's joint chain, thicker at the hip and thinner near the foot, using the three-point chain (root, knee, foot) so the span and tip names line up correctly. I'm also planning foot pads positioned at each limb's terminal joint point, and double-checking that the limb function returns the joint positions in the right format for the sweep and placement calls.

I'm verifying the yaw-based transform maps local forward/left directions to correct world-space directions, checking both 0 and π cases, plus confirming the mirrored leg offsets and joint aim points align correctly with the camel's local coordinate system.

Writing module imports...

Adding more type imports...

I'm prefixing unused params with underscores to satisfy the typechecker, then starting the module with metadata describing an oasis diorama scene with a pool surrounded by desert terrain.

Still writing sand coloring...

The sand disc includes its cylinder sides, so the paint function covers them too since it receives position and normal everywhere. With the top face normal pointing straight up, the cel shading lights it well, keeping the sand looking consistent across the whole shape.

Now I'm working through the color palette: flat tones for the wooden plinth and its rim, a glowing cyan for the water, mottled earthy hues for the rocks using cel shading, and warm browns for the trunk and its rings, moving into greens for the leaves.

Finishing up the palette with coconut brown, grass texture colors, canvas/red/teal/gold accents, countershaded camel coat, a dark nose tone, and brass. Then I'm defining the camel construction function with a typed Pose and position helper that accounts for yaw rotation, setting up the Builder-based structure for assembling the camel model.

Writing spine chain and body loft...

Defining neck chain spline...

For spine.tip, I should guard against null by falling back to the last joint in spine.joints, so the parent reference stays type-safe.

I'm now sweeping the neck with a radius tapering from 0.2 at the chest down to 0.13 at the tip, then defining the head joint from the neck's last joint before lofting the skull shape.

For the skull, I'm adding loft stations with varying widths and heights to carve out the head's rounded profile, binding it to the head joint rigidly. Then I'm adding eye decals mirrored on each side, projecting them onto the skull surface near the widest head station and sizing them small and oval-shaped.

Now I'm defining the ear profile as a curved outline with a sharp point near the tip.

I'm worried the "sharp" literal type won't infer correctly in the array, so I'll simplify by typing EAR as a plain array of number pairs and skipping the sharp-corner marker, relying on smoothing to give a rounded ear shape instead.

Now I'm looping over left/right sides, extruding the EAR outline at a point computed relative to the head joint, oriented along forward and up-back axes, with a small thickness and smoothing of 1 to round the edges, colored as the coat and bound to the head joint.

For the ear outline itself, I'm defining a leaf-like shape with a narrow base and curved tip using five points, roughly 0.3 units tall and 0.12 wide, which with smoothing should look like a rounded animal ear.

I'm double-checking the ear placement logic — the left/right offset, forward/up directions, and vertical position relative to the head joint all check out, putting the ears along the upper flanks of the skull near its top. Then I move to placing a nose: a small sphere bound to the head joint, offset forward and slightly down, landing it near the front of the muzzle around station four's radius.

Next I set up a jaw joint parented to the head, aimed toward the front of the muzzle, and add a lower-jaw capsule part colored to match the coat, keeping things simple by skipping extra details like a tongue or mouth line. With the head finished, I shift to building the legs — sketching out a helper function that takes a side, z-position, and parent joint/chain to generate each leg, along with a hind-leg flag for variation.

I'm working out the hind leg geometry: placing the hip root, estimating the foot position under the body, and solving for where the hock/knee should bend backward using triangle-based IK math so the stance looks natural, even if it ends up a bit exaggerated and whimsical like a real camel's deep hock.

For the front leg I'm doing the same reachability check, confirming the limb segment lengths comfortably span the distance between hip and foot, with the knee bending forward this time. I'm then setting up the leg chain structure with named joints (hip, knee, foot) so each limb can be built and animated consistently.

Now I'm defining the leg sweep geometry with a tapered radius from hip to foot, then attaching hoof cylinders at the foot joint position for each leg.

Moving on to the tail, I'm setting up its chain using a catmull-rom spline through several control points running back from the hip.

Hind legs parent to the Back joint, and front legs should parent to Withers, which checks out with the four-joint spine array. For the saddle blanket, I'm placing a flattened box over the Mid joint with a blanket texture applied.

Checking the body's loft profile at that z-position, the body top interpolates to roughly 1.63, so the blanket box sitting at 1.63–1.69 lands right on the body's back without floating — the width also matches reasonably against the body's ~0.78 width at that station.

Maybe skip the blanket entirely, or repurpose it as a small decal trim on the neck instead, but that seems too minor. I'll instead drape it lower as a saddle blanket hanging along the camel's flank, which feels more natural for the body shape.

Checking the hump placement against the blanket box — hump bottom at 1.4 falls within the blanket's range, so the hump pushes through the saddle blanket, which actually reads as realistic. I'll shift the blanket further back along z to better fit the hump position.

Adjusting blanket width to 0.7 so it properly spans the hindquarters at that narrower body station. Tallying up the total parts per camel — spine, hump, neck, head, eyes, ears, nose, jaw, legs with hooves, tail, blanket — landing around 25 pieces total, which feels right before moving into posing.

For the drinking pose, I'm rotating the neck's first joint downward and forward so the whole chain above it (upper neck, head, jaw, eyes, ears, nose) follows since they're skinned to these joints. Working out the resulting head position: starting from the neck joint around y=1.42, z=0.34, rotating along a down-and-forward direction brings the head down to roughly y=0.86, z=0.79, putting the muzzle close to ground level as intended for a drinking stance.

Then I realize I've been computing in local coordinates and forgot the sand's actual ground offset — the camel's legs are built assuming floor at y=0.07, but the sand surface sits at y=0.42, so I need a global GROUND offset added to every y coordinate in my position helper function, along with tents, palms, and dunes all needing that same base offset. I'm reworking the muzzle-height calculation for the drinking camel to land right at the pool's water surface (~0.44), re-deriving the local head and neck1 heights (around 2.02 and 1.42 respectively before the ground offset) to get the final absolute position right.

But then I hit a snag: pivoting the neck downward only drops the head to around absolute 1.23, way above the water at 0.5 — the 0.78-length neck segment just isn't long enough to bridge that gap with a single pivot, meaning I either need a longer neck, a lower chest/leg stance, or to reposition the pool closer to the camel's body to make the geometry work.

I decide to abandon the drinking pose entirely and just have the camels standing normally, maybe with heads slightly turned for variety using a yaw rotation on the neck joint rather than a steep downward pitch. I'm also noticing the overall camel height comes out taller than a real dromedary (around 2.7m vs 2.0m), so I should scale things down a bit.

Redesigning with lower proportions: shorter legs, body center around 1.0-1.08, hump top near 1.9, chest and head joints repositioned so total height with ears lands closer to 2.5m, giving a more realistic dromedary silhouette. Now recalculating the spine and joint coordinates with these reduced values...
